content.text: Gears this small do not forgive a shaking hand, so the workshop taught me stillness before it taught me skill. The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match.

My master's own hands shook by the end, and he taught the last lessons entirely by voice. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats. An old debt of kindness is rarely called in outright, only quietly remembered.

A pocket watch carries its owner's habits in its wear pattern, if you know where on the case to look. The bread rose slowly in the cold kitchen, and the whole house smelled the better for waiting. A traveller's stories improve with each telling, a fact both teller and listener quietly agree to overlook.

The apprenticeship ran seven years, though I only remember, clearly, about seven months of it. The workshop closed for the season the way it always did, mid-sentence, with a job left half finished. An old road, no longer maintained, is still walkable long after it stops being useful.

Small gears taught me that precision and patience are, more often than not, the same virtue wearing two names. The frost patterns on the window that January were, by common agreement, the finest anyone could recall. A letter home, written honestly, is harder to write than any other kind.

I still keep that first, over-fast movement on my own shelf now, for reasons my master would have understood. The village kept its own time, twenty minutes behind the railway, and saw no reason to change. An empty ledger page is, in its way, as informative as a full one.

A watchmaker's apprentice learns to apologise to no one for the time a good repair takes. The last apple of the season always tasted, everyone agreed, a little better for being the last. A long friendship survives more silence than most people think it can.

The loupe made the workshop's whole world the size of a coin, and I found I preferred it that size. The workshop lamp burned oil at a rate its owner tracked more carefully than his own accounts. An old map, however wrong, still tells you what someone once believed to be true.

My master called an unfinished repair a promise, and did not consider the day done until every promise was kept. The harbor bell rang for fog more nights that year than anyone could remember from before. A garden planted in hope outlives, more often than not, the gardener's doubts about it.

A study in small gears ends, eventually, in a study of the larger, slower gear a life turns out to be. The evening chores went faster with two people than with one, though neither said so aloud. An old coat pocket, searched later, tells you where its owner had actually been.

The first movement I ever finished ran eleven minutes fast a day, and I loved it anyway for being mine. The workshop's youngest apprentice asked more questions than the others combined, and was rarely told to stop. A river in flood forgives nothing and remembers everything, at least until the next flood.

A watchmaker's apprentice learns patience from gears before he learns it from people, which is the correct order. The last light in the house went out later that winter than in any winter before it. An unopened letter waits with a patience its writer rarely shared.

Small gears forgive nothing, my master used to say, and count that as a mercy rather than a cruelty. The bakery's ovens stayed warm long after closing, heating the whole street a little further into the evening. A long-kept promise is worth more, if anything, for having been long-kept.

I spent a season on a single balance wheel and considered the season well spent. The harbor emptied of boats by storm warning and filled again, cautiously, the following noon. An old friend recognized across a crowded market is a small, entirely disproportionate joy.

The workshop smelled of oil and brass filings, a smell I have never managed to dislike. The workshop's ledgers, taken together, told a quieter story than either the profits or the losses alone. A garden wall built by hand outlasts, as a rule, the hands that built it.

A study in small gears is really a study in attention, dressed up in tweezers and a loupe. Time moves at a different pace when there is work enough to fill it entirely. A room remembers its last occupant longer than most people expect.

My master kept broken watches on a shelf as a kind of memorial to lessons he had already learned the hard way. The kettle took its usual three minutes, and in that time the whole morning seemed to settle. Distance is measured in more than miles once you have walked enough of it yourself.

The first movement taught me more by failing than any movement since has taught me by working. A garden left untended for a season still remembers, mostly, what it was planted to become. The clock in the hall ran two minutes fast for as long as anyone could remember, and no one corrected it.

A watch that runs true is, in the end, just a very small, very patient argument won honestly. Patience is easier to recommend than to practise, a fact every teacher of it eventually admits. The correspondence between old friends thins with distance but rarely stops outright.

I learned to hear a bad escapement before I learned to see one, which surprised my master more than it surprised me. A machine well maintained will forgive a great many small mistakes; one neglected forgives none. Quiet, in the right house, is not an absence of sound but a particular kind of company.

The weather that season did exactly what the almanac predicted, which surprised everyone involved. A long walk clarifies more than a long conversation, in my limited experience of both. The light in late afternoon has a habit of making ordinary rooms look briefly important.

Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac.

Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it.

Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be.

The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why.

A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household.
